3.text: which a prize is offered to the winner. Every one who has taken three

4.text: jumps successfully may stop, and wait his turn to compete with a performer

5.text: who has achieved a similar success. I was told by the people that the “toss-

10.text: Like the reindeer-races of the Reindeer Chukchee, the “tossing on walrus-

11.text: hide” of the Maritime people takes on the character of a sport, and is fre-

12.text: quently arranged merely for amusement, without connection with any religious

13.text: or superstitious purpose. From the Maritime people the “tossing on walrus-

14.text: hide” spread to the Reindeer Chukchee, among whom it is, however, much

15.text: less in use, and serves only for a merry social exercise.

16.text: Races. — Racing with dogs by the Maritime Chukchee is much less

17.text: frequent than reindeer-racing by the Reindeer Chukchee. The dog-races occur

18.text: chiefly in spring, and have no connection with the ordinary ceremonials. The

19.text: race is accompanied with a small sacrifice thrown into a small fire and towards

20.text: the principal “directions.” It is followed by a foot-race of men and women and

21.text: by a wrestling-contest. The Asiatic Eskimo arrange the dog-races similarly,

22.text: but they still attach the dogs in the old way, — several abreast, with a

23.text: leader in the front on a long trace.¹

24.text: Fig. 284, copied from a native sketch, represents a foot-race of Maritime

25.text: Chukchee, which was performed in connection with the “genuine thanksgiving

26.text: ceremonial.” Six young men are taking part in the race. Two “masters of

27.text: the race” are looking on. A coil of thong and a bunch of leaf-tobacco are

28.text: suspended on two short sticks as prizes for the race. Three heads and two

29.text: sacrificial vessels are set on the ground. The heads are those of the walrus,

30.text: a white fox, and a hare.
